```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(gapminder)
library(modelr)
library(broom)
```

The challenge:

Life expectancy for a country is the mean length of life over the
people of that country. Using the variables life expectancy (`lifeExp`)
and population (`pop`) of a country, from the `gapminder` dataset:

1. Derive a formula to compute the life expectancy of a continent (a
   group of countries).
2. Plot how life expectancy changed over time for each continent.
3. Do the same for the whole planet.

```{r}
gapminder
```

Each row is one country in one year, with its `lifeExp` and `pop`
already recorded. There is no `lifeExp` column for a continent or for
the world, we have to build one ourselves.

# Part 1: deriving the formula

## Why a simple average across countries is wrong

The naive approach is to just average `lifeExp` across all countries
in a continent for a given year:

$$
L_{\text{naive}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} L_i
$$

This treats every country equally, no matter whether it has 1 million
or 1 billion people. We can see this bias directly in the data: a
tiny country gets exactly the same weight as a population giant.

```{r}
gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia") %>%
  select(country, pop, lifeExp) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop))
```

China and India alone hold the overwhelming majority of Asia's
population in this table, yet a plain average of the `lifeExp` column
would let Bahrain or Bhutan move the "continent average" just as much
as China does. That can't be right if we want a number that reflects
how long the *typical person* on that continent lives.

## The correct formula: a population-weighted mean

Life expectancy is a *rate* (years per person); population is an
*extensive* quantity (a count of people). To combine a rate correctly
across groups of different sizes, each country's `lifeExp` must be
weighted by its share of the continent's total population:

$$
L_{\text{continent}} =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i \, L_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i}
$$

This is not an ad hoc fix, it falls directly out of what life
expectancy means. If $L_i$ is the average lifespan of the $P_i$ people
in country $i$, then $P_i L_i$ is the total number of life-years
lived in that country. Summing $P_i L_i$ over every country in the
continent and dividing by the continent's total population gives the
average lifespan across *every individual on the continent*,
regardless of which country they live in, exactly
$L_{\text{continent}}$ above. The same formula, applied over every
country in the world instead of just one continent, gives the
population-weighted life expectancy of the whole planet.

We implement this with a single `group_by()` + `summarise()`:

```{r}
weighted_lifeexp <- function(lifeExp, pop) {
  sum(lifeExp * pop) / sum(pop)
}
```

# Part 2: life expectancy over time, by continent

```{r}
continent_lifeexp <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarise(
    lifeExp_weighted = weighted_lifeexp(lifeExp, pop),
    lifeExp_naive     = mean(lifeExp),
    pop_total         = sum(pop)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

continent_lifeexp
```

## The main plot

```{r}
ggplot(continent_lifeexp, aes(year, lifeExp_weighted, color = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Population-weighted life expectancy by continent, 1952–2007",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Life expectancy (years)",
    color = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The plot shows the pattern we'd expect from first principles: every
continent trends upward over time, but Africa starts far below the
others and the gap between continents narrows over the decades
(convergence), rather than all the lines staying parallel.

## Does weighting actually matter here?

We can check this directly by comparing the naive (unweighted) average
to the population-weighted one, continent by continent:

```{r}
continent_lifeexp %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(lifeExp_weighted, lifeExp_naive),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "lifeExp"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, lifeExp, color = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent) +
  labs(
    title = "Weighted vs. naive (unweighted) continent life expectancy",
    x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The two methods diverge most on continents made of countries with very
unequal populations (Asia, dominated by China and India; the Americas,
dominated by the US and Brazil), and they're closest where countries
are more similar in size. This confirms the reasoning from Part 1:
weighting only matters when population is unevenly distributed across
the group being aggregated.

## A closer look: dips and shocks

Following the same approach as the "many simple models" case study,
fitting a linear trend of `lifeExp` against `year` for each country
and inspecting the residuals, reveals *where* the continent-level
dips actually come from:

```{r}
country_models <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(country, continent) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ lm(lifeExp ~ year, data = .x)),
    data  = map2(data, model, ~ add_residuals(.x, .y))
  ) %>%
  unnest(data)

ggplot(country_models, aes(year, resid, group = country)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ continent) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals of lifeExp ~ year, by country, faceted by continent",
    x = "Year", y = "Residual (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Africa stands out from every other continent: several countries show a
sharp mid-series collapse away from a simple linear improvement. This
is the HIV/AIDS mortality shock of the 1990s, and because it hit
several populous African countries at once, it is exactly the kind of
event that shows up as a visible dent in the population-weighted
continent curve above, even though it affected only one continent.

# Part 3: the same formula for the whole planet

The planet is simply the special case of "one continent" containing
every country on Earth. The identical weighted-mean formula applies,
we just drop `continent` from the grouping:

```{r}
world_lifeexp <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    lifeExp_weighted = weighted_lifeexp(lifeExp, pop),
    pop_total         = sum(pop)
  )

world_lifeexp
```

```{r}
ggplot(world_lifeexp, aes(year, lifeExp_weighted)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "black") +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Population-weighted world life expectancy, 1952–2007",
    x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Checking internal consistency: country-level vs. continent-level aggregation

The weighted-mean formula has a useful consistency property (a form of
the law of total expectation): we should get the same world average
whether we aggregate directly over every country, or aggregate
continents first and then combine those continent totals. Let's verify
this numerically:

```{r}
world_from_continents <- continent_lifeexp %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(lifeExp_from_continents = weighted_lifeexp(lifeExp_weighted, pop_total))

world_lifeexp %>%
  left_join(world_from_continents, by = "year") %>%
  mutate(difference = lifeExp_weighted - lifeExp_from_continents)
```

The `difference` column is (up to floating-point rounding) zero for
every year: aggregating country \(\to\) world directly and aggregating
country \(\to\) continent \(\to\) world give identical results, exactly
as the formula predicts.

## Comparing the world curve to the continents

```{r}
continent_lifeexp %>%
  select(continent, year, lifeExp_weighted) %>%
  bind_rows(
    world_lifeexp %>% mutate(continent = "World") %>%
      select(continent, year, lifeExp_weighted)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, lifeExp_weighted, color = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "World life expectancy vs. each continent",
    x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)", color = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

As expected, the world curve sits between the continent curves,
pulled closest to Asia and the Americas, the continents holding the
largest shares of world population, and it shows the same long-run
upward trend as the continents individually, smoothed because a shock
confined to one continent is diluted by the rest of the world's
population when averaged globally.

# Conclusion

1. Life expectancy must be aggregated with population as weights, 
   $L_{\text{continent}} = \dfrac{\sum_i P_i L_i}{\sum_i P_i}$,  not
   with a plain average, because life expectancy is a per-person rate
   and countries differ hugely in how many people that rate applies
   to.
2. Computing this for each continent and year shows a long-run upward
   trend, convergence between continents, and a sharp dip in Africa
   in the 1990s driven by HIV/AIDS, visible in the residuals of simple
   per-country linear models.
3. The identical formula, applied over every country on Earth, gives
   the world's life expectancy, and this is numerically consistent
   whether computed directly from countries or in two steps through
   continents, confirming the formula is internally coherent across
   levels of aggregation.
